map.External integrations: 6 services (FMG, FortiGate, Entra/Graph, AD/LDAP, WinRM, vCenter) + 16 fetch sites

findings.title: Backup and restore are not TimescaleDB-aware, so the disaster-recovery path is unvalidated
findings.risk: Every documented production install enables TimescaleDB (docs/INSTALL.md installs timescaledb-2-postgresql-15, and timescaleService.ts converts 21 sample and rollup tables into hypertables with compression policies). Backup runs a plain pg_dump and restore pipes the dump into `psql --single-transaction`. Neither calls `timescaledb_pre_restore()` or `timescaledb_post_restore()`, which Timescale documents as required around a restore: without them, hypertable catalog rows and chunk metadata restore in the wrong order and the restore either aborts or produces hypertables whose chunks are invisible. Nothing in the repo exercises a restore, so the failure only shows up the day it is needed.
findings.fix:
Wrap the restore in the documented Timescale sequence before shipping. In the restore handler, after opening psql, run:
psql "$CONN" -c 'SELECT timescaledb_pre_restore();'
then stream the dump, then
psql "$CONN" -c 'SELECT timescaledb_post_restore();'
On the backup side, prefer `pg_dump --format=custom` so pg_restore can order objects, and add `--exclude-table-data` for the internal `_timescaledb_internal` chunk tables only if you adopt Timescale's documented chunk-level procedure instead. Then prove it: a CI or staging job that takes a backup of a Timescale-enabled DB, restores it into an empty database, and asserts that `SELECT count(*) FROM timescaledb_information.hypertables` and a per-table row count both match the source.
findings.confirm: Confirm with the DBA which Timescale version prod runs, since the supported dump/restore procedure differs between 2.x minor lines. This must be validated by a human against a real Timescale install before it is relied on.
findings.note: Fixed and VERIFIED: restore wrapped in timescaledb_pre_restore()/post_restore() in three separate psql sessions, post_restore in a finally. TimescaleDB 2.28.3 was installed into the dev Postgres (compose.dev.yml now uses timescale/timescaledb:latest-pg15) and tests/integration/backupRestore.test.ts passes all 6 cases against it, including both round trips and the leaves-the-DB-usable-after-a-failed-restore case. Running it surfaced a second, pre-existing defect now also fixed: --clean --if-exists invalidates every open connection, so the restore reported success and the app then threw 'could not open relation with OID <n>' on arbitrary queries. restoreBackup now recycles the pool and the route returns restartRequired.

findings.title: Manual backup route is synchronous and holds the whole dump in memory three times
findings.risk: The handler calls `execSync(pg_dump ...)` with a 120000 ms timeout, then `readFileSync(tmpFile)`, then `gzipSync(payload)`, then encrypts into another Buffer, then `res.end(payload)`. execSync blocks the web role's single event loop for the entire dump, so every session, agent sample push and WebSocket heartbeat stalls until it finishes. docs/INSTALL.md sizes the DB volume at 50 GB recommended, and setupRoutes.ts warns below RECOMMENDED_DB_FREE_GB = 50, so the dump is expected to be gigabytes: the 120 s cap fails it outright at that size, and if it does complete, readFileSync plus gzipSync plus the cipher output puts three copies of a multi-gigabyte payload in the heap and OOMs the process. The result is that backup silently stops working exactly when the database is big enough to matter.
findings.note: Fixed: streamed pg_dump -> gzip -> optional cipher -> file in services/backupService.ts; route streams the file back. execSync/readFileSync/gzipSync gone; fixed 120s cap replaced by a no-output watchdog.

findings.title: Device, integration and delivery-channel secrets are stored in plaintext in Postgres
findings.risk: credentialService.ts states the design outright: "plaintext at rest, masked at" read time. Credential.config, Integration.config and NotificationChannel.config are plain Json columns holding SNMP community strings, WinRM passwords, SSH passwords and SSH private keys, FortiManager and FortiGate API keys, the Entra client secret, vCenter credentials, SMTP and M365 secrets, Slack and Teams webhook URLs, and the Web Push VAPID private key. Masking happens only on the API read path, so anyone with a psql session, a read replica, a stolen volume snapshot, or one backup file holds the credentials to the entire managed network. The backup passphrase is optional (validateBackupPassword accepts null as "a legitimate choice"), so the default download is an unencrypted dump of all of it, and any custom role granted serverSettingsData read can fetch it from GET /server-settings/database/backups/:id/download.
findings.confirm: Confirm with IT which key source is approved for this app (Key Vault reference versus env-delivered key) before implementing, and confirm whether the org accepts encrypt-at-rest on the volume as a compensating control for the interim.
findings.note: Fixed: per-value AES-256-GCM sealing at the Prisma-extension seam (utils/secretBox.ts + utils/configSecretFields.ts + db.ts), key from POLARIS_SECRET_KEY, backfillSecretEncryption job converts existing rows. VERIFIED against the dev Postgres: the raw stored value is ciphertext while reads return plaintext, and the no-key path still stores plaintext (pre-feature behavior). Key source still needs IT sign-off (Key Vault vs env-delivered).

findings.title: Docker migrate container exits 0 after a failed migration, defeating the dependency gate
findings.risk: The entrypoint runs `if ! npx --no-install prisma migrate deploy; then echo WARN ... continuing anyway; fi`, then falls through to `if ROLE = migrate: exit 0`. docker-compose.yml gates web, monitor and discovery on `migrate: condition: service_completed_successfully`, so a migration that fails still satisfies the gate and the whole stack comes up against a stale schema. Prisma then throws `column "<name>" does not exist` on the affected tables at runtime instead of the stack refusing to start, and the operator sees a healthy-looking `docker compose up` on a half-migrated database. docs/INSTALL.md presents this compose file as a supported production shape.
findings.fix:
Fail the container so the orchestrator's gate means something:
if ! npx --no-install prisma migrate deploy; then
  echo "[entrypoint] FATAL: prisma migrate deploy failed" >&2
  exit 1
fi
This matches how the systemd path already behaves (polaris-migrate.service is Type=oneshot and the app units Require= it) and how applyUpdate in src/services/updateService.ts already handles it (failUpdate on step 5, no restart).
findings.note: Fixed: docker-entrypoint.sh exits 1 on a failed migrate deploy, so compose's service_completed_successfully gate means something again.

findings.title: Subnet creation checks for overlap outside any transaction and has no backing DB constraint
findings.risk: createSubnet reads all sibling CIDRs with `prisma.subnet.findMany`, tests them with cidrOverlaps, then calls `prisma.subnet.create` as a separate statement, with no transaction and no row locking. allocateNextSubnet has the same shape: it reads the sibling set, computes the next free CIDR, then delegates to createSubnet. The Subnet model carries only indexes on cidr and blockId, no unique or exclusion constraint, so two concurrent POSTs of the same or overlapping CIDR both pass the check and both insert. Business rules 1 and 2 are then violated silently, and once two subnets overlap, every downstream IP allocation across them can hand the same address to two owners. This is the core IPAM invariant, and it has no enforcement below the application layer.
findings.note: Fixed: per-block pg_advisory_xact_lock + in-transaction overlap re-check in createSubnetRowChecked/lockBlockForSubnetWrites; UNIQUE index on (blockId, cidr) as backstop; allocateNextSubnet retries a lost race. VERIFIED against the dev Postgres, including that a create bypassing the seam is rejected by the index.

findings.title: Device Map site and topology reads are not gated on the deviceMap permission
findings.risk: GET /map/sites, GET /map/sites/:id/topology and GET /map/sites/:id/topology/search carry no requirePermission call, and router.ts mounts /map with no gate either. Only the two layout writes check deviceMap=write. Any authenticated session, and any bearer token bound to any role including one with deviceMap set to none, reads every FortiGate hostname, its coordinates, and its full topology (managed switches, access points, wireless stations, LLDP neighbours, MCLAG peers). The nav table in public/js/app.js gives the Device Map entry no perm either, so the only thing that looks like access control here is the UI, and it is not applied. router.ts line 139 documents a floor that the code does not implement: "the rest of /map is read-only and open to any authenticated user with at least deviceMap=read".
findings.confirm: Intent decides this. Confirm whether the Device Map is meant to be visible to every authenticated user (in which case remove the deviceMap read level from the docs and the function-key description) or whether deviceMap=none is meant to hide site inventory. The function key exists and the router comment claims a read floor, which is why this is flagged.
findings.note: Fixed: deviceMap=read floor on the /map mount (main router + dash listener), page gate on /map.html, nav perm, and the siteMap widget re-gated onto deviceMap. All four seeded non-admin roles already carry deviceMap=read, so this is non-breaking.

findings.title: Bulk allocate is atomic but not isolated, so its overlap re-check can be raced
findings.risk: bulkAllocate correctly wraps the whole batch in `prisma.$transaction` and re-reads the sibling set inside it, and its comment says this is so "concurrent allocations don't race with us". At Postgres READ COMMITTED, which is the default and is not overridden anywhere in the codebase, that re-read does not see another in-flight transaction's uncommitted inserts and takes no locks on the rows it is reasoning about. Two concurrent bulk allocations against the same block can both pick the same free anchor region and both commit, producing an overlapping template pair. The transaction guarantees all-or-nothing, which is what the comment describes, but not the mutual exclusion the invariant needs.
findings.note: Fixed: bulkAllocate takes the same per-block advisory lock as the single-row seam inside its existing transaction.

findings.title: Database URL with password is interpolated into a shell command and can be returned to the caller
findings.risk: The backup handler builds `execSync(\`pg_dump "${connUrl}" ...\`)` where connUrl is the full DATABASE_URL or POLARIS_DB_DIRECT_URL including the password. Two exposures follow. The command line is visible to any local user via `ps aux` and lands in any process listing, audit trail or core dump for the duration of the dump. And on failure the handler throws `new AppError(500, "pg_dump failed: " + (err.stderr?.toString() || err.message))`: Node sets err.message to "Command failed: <the full command>", so whenever stderr is empty, which is what a timeout kill produces, the connection string with the password is returned in the HTTP response body and rendered in the UI. The restore path passes connUrl as an argv element to spawn (line 489), which is not shell-injectable but has the same ps visibility.
findings.note: Fixed: connection passed via libpq PG* env vars (utils/pgEnv.ts), never argv; child-process stderr logged, never returned to the caller.

findings.title: Pre-update backup failure is non-fatal and reported to the operator as a completed step
findings.risk: The pre-update backup is wrapped so that any failure calls `setStep(0, "done", "Backup skipped: " + message)` and the update continues. Step 0 renders as done, not as a warning or a failure, so the Application Updates card shows a green step while the only rollback point for the update has silently not been created. The update then proceeds through `git pull`, `npm ci` and `prisma migrate deploy`, and migrations are not reversible: if a migration or the new code goes wrong there is nothing to restore. Given OPS-01, the backup may also be unrestorable even when it is taken, so the operator has two independent reasons to believe they are protected when they are not.
findings.note: Fixed: a failed pre-update backup now marks the step failed and ABORTS the update; continuing requires the operator to tick 'proceed even if the backup fails' (allowWithoutBackup), which is audited.

findings.title: Fleet-wide DNS sweep does serial lookups and one UPDATE per asset inside a request handler
findings.risk: POST /assets/dns-lookup loads every non-excluded asset with an IP, then loops `for (const asset of needsPrimary)` doing one `await resolver.reverse()` followed by one `await prisma.asset.update()` per asset, with no concurrency cap and no batching. The associated-IP loop immediately below it (line 3081) does the same. At the 2000-asset fleet size CLAUDE.md requires every change to be reasoned about, that is thousands of serial DNS round trips plus thousands of individual UPDATE round trips inside a single HTTP request: the request outlives any nginx proxy_read_timeout, the operator sees a gateway error while the sweep keeps running, and a slow or unreachable resolver multiplies the whole thing by the per-lookup timeout. The sibling per-asset route at line 3145 already collects its updates and applies them in one `prisma.$transaction`, so the correct pattern exists a few lines away.
findings.note: Fixed: bounded lookup pool + batched transactional writes in POST /assets/dns-lookup.

findings.title: Bulk quarantine accepts an unbounded id list and pushes to devices serially
findings.risk: POST /assets/bulk-quarantine and POST /assets/bulk-quarantine/release validate `ids: z.array(z.string()).min(1)` with no upper bound, then loop `for (const id of input.ids)` awaiting quarantineAsset / releaseQuarantine one at a time. Each iteration performs live FortiGate device I/O. A 2000-id selection is therefore 2000 serial device writes held inside one HTTP request, which will exceed the proxy timeout and leave the operator with no reliable view of what actually landed. The sibling POST /assets/bulk-monitor at line 827 was already converted from a per-asset loop to a single updateMany with the comment "Was 1000 sequential round trips, is now one statement", so the scale concern is already recognised on this route file.
findings.note: Fixed: bulk-quarantine and release cap at 500 ids and drain through a bounded pool.

findings.title: No process-level unhandledRejection or uncaughtException handler in any role
findings.risk: There is no `process.on("unhandledRejection")` or `process.on("uncaughtException")` anywhere in src/. The units run plain `/usr/bin/node dist/index.js` with no --unhandled-rejections flag, so Node 20's default is to throw and terminate. The individual paths are disciplined (logEvent swallows internally, every job tick is wrapped in try/catch, the floating prisma updates in agentChannelService carry .catch), so this is a missing last resort rather than a live crash, but there is no floor: one escaped rejection anywhere in 322 files takes down a whole web, monitor or discovery process, and all the operator gets is Node's bare stack trace on stderr. There is no pino line, no Event row, and no capacity signal, and Restart=on-failure brings the process back so the incident can repeat unseen.
findings.note: Fixed: utils/crashHandlers.ts installs unhandledRejection/uncaughtException handlers from src/index.ts, logs a structured fatal line with the role, increments polaris_process_crash_total, and exits 70. Grafana panels + README bullet added.

findings.title: No scheduled backup exists, and backups land next to the application they protect
findings.risk: The only two ways a backup is ever created are an operator clicking Backup on the Maintenance tab and the pre-update backup, which OPS-06 shows is skippable. There is no backup job in src/jobs/ (57 files, none of them a backup), no cron or systemd timer in deploy/, and docs/INSTALL.md never tells the operator to schedule one; it only sizes the volume for `data/backups/`. Backups therefore accumulate on the same host and often the same volume as the application, and the inventory of them lives in a `backup_history` Setting row capped at 50 entries inside the very database being backed up. A host loss takes the database and every backup of it at once, and an install where nobody remembers to click the button has no recovery point at all.
findings.fix: Ship the schedule rather than documenting the intent. Add a `scheduledBackup` job to src/jobs/ following the maintenanceScheduler shape (interval tick, try/catch, runInstrumentedJob) driven by a `backupSchedule` Setting row edited on the Maintenance tab: cadence, retention count, passphrase source, and a target directory the operator can point at a mounted share. Then add a section to docs/INSTALL.md that states the retention policy, where the copies go off-host, and how to verify one restores, referencing the OPS-01 restore procedure.
findings.confirm: Confirm with IT whether an existing enterprise backup product already covers this Postgres instance. If it does, the fix is to document that and drop the in-app scheduler rather than build a second mechanism.
findings.note: Fixed: backupScheduleService + scheduledBackup job + GET|PUT /database/backup-schedule + a Maintenance-tab card, default-off, with retention and an off-host copy directory. INSTALL.md gained a 'Backups: set this up on day one' section. Still worth confirming whether an enterprise backup product already covers this instance.

findings.title: Backup and restore have zero automated coverage
findings.risk: 194 test files cover permission gates, reservations, subnets, sample rollup, maintenance schedules, agent ingest and the dash server, but nothing touches the backup or restore routes: grep for `database/backup`, `database/restore` or `pg_dump` across tests/ returns nothing. tests/unit/backupPassword.test.ts covers only passphrase validation. The one path whose failure is unrecoverable is therefore the one path with no test, which is why OPS-01 and OPS-02 could both be true at the same time without anything flagging it.
findings.fix: Add one integration test that closes the loop against the podman dev Postgres the suite already uses: POST /server-settings/database/backup with a passphrase, assert the POLARIS\0 magic header and a non-zero size, then POST /server-settings/database/restore with that file into a scratch database and assert a known row count survives. Assert the same for the unencrypted variant. If the dev container can have the timescaledb extension enabled, make that the default fixture so the OPS-01 gap is covered by the same test. Run it with --no-file-parallelism like the rest of the DB-touching suite.
findings.note: Fixed and RUNNING: tests/unit/backupEnvelope.test.ts pins the on-disk format (runs everywhere) and tests/integration/backupRestore.test.ts does the real round trip. With TimescaleDB installed in the dev stack and the suite run inside the app container (which has pg_dump/psql), the whole suite is 201/201 files and 2538/2538 tests with ZERO skips - previously 31 files / 289 tests skipped.

findings.title: Conflict resolution records no actor for bearer-token callers
findings.risk: The accept, merge and reject handlers pass `req.session?.username` as the actor into acceptConflict, mergeAssetConflict and rejectConflict. Those routes are reachable by bearer tokens, which pass the same hasPermission("discoveryConflicts", "write") gate but carry no session, so username is undefined and the resulting audit trail attributes the resolution to nobody. Conflict resolution overwrites asset and reservation fields and absorbs ghost assets, so this is exactly the class of mutation the audit log exists for. src/api/middleware/auth.ts already exports requestActor(req) for this, and the assets and reservations route files use it.
findings.note: Fixed: conflicts.ts resolves the actor through requestActor(req), so bearer-token resolutions are attributed.

findings.title: Pre-update backup is read entirely into memory just to measure its size
findings.risk: `const sizeBytes = existsSync(backupFile) ? readFileSync(backupFile).length : 0;` loads the whole gzipped dump into the heap only to take its length, then discards it. The dump itself was correctly streamed to disk on the lines above, so this single line reintroduces the memory profile the streaming avoided, on a multi-gigabyte file, at the exact moment the process is about to run npm ci and a TypeScript build.
findings.note: Fixed: statSync(f).size replaces readFileSync(f).length for the pre-update backup size.

findings.title: The in-app update pipeline has no coverage beyond train selection
findings.risk: applyUpdate is the highest-blast-radius code path in the repo: it takes a backup, repoints the git remote, checks out a tag or fast-forwards a branch, runs npm ci, regenerates the Prisma client, builds, runs migrate deploy, syncs systemd units and the nginx config, and restarts polaris.target. The only test that touches updateService is tests/unit/updateTrain.test.ts, which covers getUpdateTrain and setUpdateTrain normalisation and nothing else. The step sequencing, the failUpdate-and-stop behaviour at each gate, and the OPS-06 backup-skip branch are all unverified, and CLAUDE.md directs operators to use this mechanism for every production deployment.
findings.fix: Test the orchestration with the shell seams stubbed rather than the shell itself. Extract the exec calls behind an injectable runner, then assert: a failure at each step calls failUpdate with that step index and never reaches the restart; a successful run advances the steps in order; the release train checks out the highest tag from `git tag --sort=-v:refname`; and the backup branch is reached before the pull. That is a handful of fast unit tests with no Docker dependency and it locks in the rollback contract the OPS-06 fix depends on.
findings.note: Fixed: tests/unit/updatePipeline.test.ts covers step sequencing, the fail-and-stop contract at each gate, the backup-abort branch, and train selection, via a _setExecRunnerForTests seam.
